lesson.grammar_point: used to + verb and would + verb for past habits and states (we used to watch, I would laugh); did you use to...?; x be used to + -ing (accustomed to)

listenings.text: Younger people don't believe me, but there was a time when you couldn't choose when to watch a series. If the new episode was on Thursday at eight, you had to be at home, in front of the TV, at eight. No pause, no rewind. And the next day, everybody would talk about it at work or at school. Did you see what Ross did? Can you believe it? We used to wait a whole week for the next episode. Today, of course, it's much easier. But I miss one thing. We used to watch the same thing at the same time as everybody else. It made us feel connected.

Nostalgia used to be seen as a problem, almost an illness. Today we know it's much more positive than that. It's a mix of happiness and a little sadness when we think about the past. Research shows that people feel more nostalgia when they're stressed, lonely, or going through a big change. That's when we go back to the old songs and the old series. And it actually helps. When we look back on good moments, we feel more connected to other people and less alone. So if you rewatch the same sitcom after a hard week, don't feel guilty. Your brain knows what it's doing.

I grew up in a small town in Australia, and every afternoon after school, I used to watch reruns of an American sitcom. My mum thought I was wasting my time. But I would repeat the lines with the characters, and I would write the best jokes in a notebook. Without noticing, I was learning how Americans really speak. Years later, when I visited New York for the first time, I was surprised. People really talked like the characters in the show! I didn't use to think TV could teach you anything. Now I'm used to recommending it to everybody who's learning English.

paras: In the 1990s, millions of families used to wait for Thursday night. They would sit on the sofa, turn on the TV and watch six friends in a coffee shop in New York. Friends ended in 2004, but it never really went away. Reruns are on TV every day, and on streaming platforms it is still one of the most watched series in the world, even by people who were not born when it started.

Why do we keep watching it? Psychologists have a name for this kind of series: a comfort show. When we are tired or stressed, the brain looks for something safe. A new series can surprise us, and surprises take energy. An old sitcom does not. We know every catchphrase, every joke and every ending, so we can relax. Nostalgia helps too: when we look back on the years when we first watched it, we remember who we used to be.

Of course, not everything is timeless. Some jokes in Friends feel outdated today, and many young viewers say so. But the friendships still feel real, and that is why the show survives. As one fan put it: “I used to watch it with my sister every week. Now I’m used to watching it alone, after work. It’s like visiting old friends.”
